subject: Agriculture
title: Chinampas of Mexico
description: A micro-lesson that makes Chinampas of Mexico usable.

hook.text: The Aztecs farmed on water. They built floating gardens on the shallow lakes around Tenochtitlan.

buildup.text: Chinampas were rectangular plots of mud and vegetation anchored by tree roots in lake bottoms.

discovery.text: Roots drew water directly from the lake. Crops never needed irrigation—they sat in their water supply.

twist.text: Chinampas were incredibly productive—up to seven harvests per year. They fed a city of 200,000 people.

climax.text: A few chinampas still operate in Xochimilco, Mexico City—living remnants of Aztec agricultural genius.

punchline.text: The Aztecs didn't irrigate their fields. They floated them.

quiz.question: What are chinampas?
options: Raised garden beds built on shallow lake beds, drawing water from below

details.summary: Chinampas are floating agricultural gardens built by the Aztecs on the lakes of central Mexico. This topic covers how these ingenious raised beds created some of the most productive farmland in pre-Columbian history and continue to operate near Mexico City today.
details.whyItMatters: Chinampas produced up to seven harvests per year, supporting the massive Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan. They demonstrate how traditional water management can achieve extraordinary productivity sustainably.
takeaways: Chinampas were built by layering aquatic vegetation, mud, and soil on lake beds
They produced nearly continuous harvests year-round using lakeside nutrient cycles
Surviving chinampas in Xochimilco are a UNESCO World Heritage Site near Mexico City

faq.question: How were chinampas constructed and used?
faq.answer: The Aztecs built rectangular raised beds in shallow lakes by layering aquatic vegetation, mud, and rich lake sediment. Willow trees anchored the edges. Crops drew moisture from the surrounding water, enabling year-round cultivation without irrigation channels.

faq.question: Why were chinampas so productive?
faq.answer: Chinampas had constant water access from surrounding canals, nutrient-rich lake mud that served as natural fertilizer, and a mild climate that allowed up to seven harvests per year of beans, squash, corn, flowers, and other crops.
